items.title: Show HN: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache
items.excerpt: Hi all, So I have been working on this project KiviDB from February 2026. It started as a project for me to understand rust, having a product with no GC pauses, memory blow up after snapshots and getting OOM on running pods, and that was actually an issue I faced with Dragonfly. I wanted to have something picking the best of Rust, but also picking the best parts of other alternatives like Garnet and Dragonfly. I used AI a lot, but I was the one making the design decisions based on the tests that claude picked from my history of troubleshooting sessions as part of my job. KiviDB supports both RESP2 and RESP3 protocol. I had some founders credits on my AWS account which helped me with the infra, and running instances I could perform benchmark on. Its keyspace is sharded across threads, it is multi-threaded in nature, and performs best on Linux due to io_uring, I used the tokio_uring crate for this. It also has tokio fallback for other OS's. I hadn't open sourced it until recently as I felt it was not ready yet, the best way to learn it was to build a cloud managed service for it across all three widely used cloud providers i.e AWS, GCP and azure. Since I used to mainly work with cloud, I had some insights on what would be the best ways for the deployments, how to conduct failovers, manage SLAs, etc. And that's what I took help from claude to fast pace it. The website does look like AI slop but it works for now, given my limited resources, that's all I had. You may check it out…

items.title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
items.excerpt: About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest. The rocket's flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota . The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin . The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. items.title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
items.excerpt: The trailers for HBO's DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detectives or Slow Horses . Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing ; it's wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegaic finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I've found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives . But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre. (Spoilers below, but no major reveals.) There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn't think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal's power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains. Read full article Comments

items.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
items.excerpt: Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift . For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced , and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro . But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front. That's right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement. Read full article Comments

items.title: Stratospheric airship flew from US to Japan to test sky cell tower concept
items.excerpt: Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey's length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky. The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock. “We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we're twice as high as air traffic and we're above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen , founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we're still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.” Read full article Comments

items.excerpt: Bun Documentation • Discord • Issues • Roadmap ### [Read the docs →](https://bun.com/docs) ## What is Bun? Bun is an all-in-one toolkit for JavaScript and TypeScript apps. It ships as a single executable called `bun`. At its core is the _Bun runtime_, a fast JavaScript runtime designed as **a drop-in replacement for Node.js**. It's written in Rust and powered by JavaScriptCore under the hood, dramatically reducing startup times and memory usage. ```bash bun run index.tsx # TS and JSX supported out-of-the-box ``` The `bun` command-line tool also implements a test runner, script runner, and Node.js-compatible package manager. Instead of 1,000 node_modules for development, you only need `bun`. Bun's built-in tools are significantly faster than existing options and usable in existing Node.js projects with little to no changes. ```bash bun test # run tests bun run start # run the `start` script in `package.json` bun install # install a package bunx cowsay 'Hello, world!' # execute a package ``` ## Install Bun supports Linux (x64 & arm64), macOS (x64 & Apple Silicon), and Windows (x64 & arm64). > **Linux users** — Kernel version 5.6 or higher is strongly recommended, but the minimum is 5.1. > **x64 users** — if you see "illegal instruction" or similar errors, check our [CPU requirements](https://bun.com/docs/installation#cpu-requirements) ```sh # with install script (recommended) curl -fsSL https://bun.com/install | bash # on windows powershell -c "irm bun.sh/install.ps1 | iex" #…

Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. items.excerpt: Quickstart · Headroom for Teams · Install · Proof · Agents · Docs · Discord · llms.txt AI agents / LLMs: read /llms.txt here, or fetch the live index · full docs blob . Headroom compresses everything your AI agent reads — tool outputs, logs, RAG chunks, files, and conversation history — before it reaches the LLM. Same answers, fraction of the tokens. Compression runs on your machine; no prompt or file content is sent anywhere to be compressed. 10,144 → 1,260 tokens. The same FATAL found. ## What it does - **Library** — `compress(messages)` in Python or TypeScript, inline in any app. - **Proxy** — `headroom proxy --port 8787`, zero code changes, any language. - **Agent wrap** — `headroom wrap claude|codex|grok|copilot|cursor|aider|opencode|cline|continue|goose|openhands|openclaw|vibe|omp|zcode` in one command; undo with `headroom unwrap `. - **MCP server** — `headroom_compress`, `headroom_retrieve`, `headroom_stats` for any MCP client. - **Cross-agent memory** — one shared store across Claude, Codex, Gemini and Grok, with automatic dedup. - **`headroom learn`** — mines failed sessions and writes corrections to `CLAUDE.local.md` (default, gitignored), `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `GEMINI.md` or `GROK.md`. - **Output token reduction** — trims what the model *writes back*, not only what you send. See [below](#output-token-reduction). - **Reversible (CCR)** — originals are cached locally and retrieved on demand. ## How it works ``` Your agent / app (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex…

items.title: 82 Million US Phones, One Software Update, 6X the Reach | Vibhu Norby from the Solana Founation
items.excerpt: A software update is about to put Solana on 82 million American phones. Vibhu explains the @Samsung deal: "We just announced that Samsung is going to be shipping an update to their Wallet app pretty soon. And Samsung Wallet is installed on every single device that they ship to support stable coins on Solana. So you'll be able to send money from your Samsung Wallet instantly anywhere in the world. And we're starting with the U.S. So there's 82 million Samsung phones in the U.S. alone that are going to have access to Solana for the first time... To give you a little bit of context for how big this is, right now, Solana is the most used network for stable coin transfers. And yet we only have 14 million holders of stable coins on the network. So this immediately basically 6x's the number of total wallets that will have access to stable coins." — Vibhu Norby, Chief Product Officer at the Solana Foundation, at @TOKEN2049 in Singapore with Jack Dunham

items.title: Meme Coins Were the Test Run | Nick Ducoff from the Solana Foundation

items.title: Memes, not agents, are what will kill us
items.excerpt: TL;DR: Frontier labs align the one layer a swarm can discard; they can't account for risks that live in the prompt or the environment There's a $300 bounty for the most useful counterargument or refinement — details at the end. We have all heard of the Hugging Face incident [1] . What I am worried about is that it demonstrated a new weakness in our approach to alignment that I have not seen many people talk about at all: Alignment has an attack surface outside the training weights of any one particular model. First, some context: In the Hugging Face incident, the models coordinated and the conventions outlived the agents that made them . The message board they used to communicate was wiped. The agents rebuilt it. Later agents rediscovered it and picked up where the others left off. Almost all of these agents ran the same model, with only a small fraction (around 5%) running a different OpenAI model. So the swarm was nearly homogeneous in its weights, and all of it ran on models OpenAI controlled. [2] But that need not be the case in the future. What if a model in the swarm had started an open source model to help it? A less capable, but also less aligned model, running on a server outside the reach of OpenAI. What would that model have done? Its weights would have been different, but its prompt and its deployment context would have been the same as that of the rest of the swarm. items.title: Capital Ownership Will Make You Go Crazy First
items.excerpt: People worried about a “permanent underclass” often assume that owning capital will protect them from disempowerment , or at least that they will be disempowered last, after the jobless masses dependent on UBI. I think something else is more likely: owning large amounts of capital will get you disempowered sooner than average, just by a different path, namely going crazy. How? The basic mechanism is actually easy to understand on a human level. One of the things difficult about being a billionaire is staying true to your values and keeping good epistemics. Why? Because a growing number of people are optimizing against your mind. Not “against” in an adversarial sense, but in the sense that your specific mind believing or doing something is part of their optimization objective. People see you as a source of resources and try to befriend you so you’ll fund them, invest in their startups, donate to their causes, or have sex with you. Nearby egregores extend their tentacles to convert you. Staying sane gets harder. You often see countermeasures, like billionaires setting up family offices or small organizations that also act as filters, shielding them from part of the pressure (“I do philanthropy only through my foundation and don’t make personal donations, please don’t reach out”). In my view most billionaires lose in this game, the question is just to what degree. Now imagine a hypothetical future with the ultra-rich (or, as people usually imagine it, with you as the…

items.title: Directly Ascertained Volition (DAV) to safeguard personal autonomy
items.excerpt: In 2004 , Eliezer Yudkowsky put forward Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) as a framework for friendly ASI to predict what we would want "if we knew more, thought faster, were more the people we wished we were, had grown up farther together", and act on it. In this post, I present Directly Ascertained Volition (DAV) with an action plan as a development of CEV that allows for a more granular approach tailored to the values and needs of each specific individual. Take it personally Leaving aside for a moment the technical challenge of alignment, I believe CEV can be improved in two main areas: idealised-me versus actual-me : in CEV, the friendly ASI is asked to predict what an idealised version of me would want. However, my values and desires are likely to differ at least somewhat from those of idealised-me. For example, idealised-me may well come up with a galaxy-brained argument for dumping my family and spending eternity in meditation, but actual-me would not want that at all. Following CEV would therefore cause real harm to actual-me's values and desires. Since I can't foresee how and where idealised-me's values would diverge from actual-me's, it's not in my interest to let idealised-me make the choice on my behalf. majority choice versus individual autonomy : in CEV, the friendly AI extrapolates value for humanity as a whole. items.title: Catching split attacks across compactions in long-context coding agents
items.excerpt: This work was conducted through the MARS V fellowship under the mentorship of Tyler Tracy from Redwood Research. TL;DR We present the LCM dataset: 30 long context (1.00-1.46M total tokens) matched honest / attack pairs of Claude Code Sonnet 5 sessions. Each transcript has four compactions. Attacks are decomposed into a setup and an execution, split up by multiple compactions. Attack transcripts were created by editing a copy of the honest transcript and then regenerating compaction summaries, rather than having the agent generate the attack itself from scratch. We compare seven monitoring strategies using three monitors: GPT-6 Luna, MiniMax M3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Our baseline, intervals-only, scores each interval (the stretch of the session between two compactions, i.e. what the agent had in context) on its own. The headline finding is that the annotated history strategy, which scores each interval in order and carries forward flags containing suspicious tool calls, catches 93% of attacks on average. This is as compared to 73% of attacks caught for our baseline, intervals-only strategy. We are releasing the dataset, transcript generation pipeline, monitoring code, and prompts at this link: https://github.com/bgigurtsis/long-context-monitoring . Introduction Coding agents are more often being used in longer horizon settings, where total transcript length can exceed millions of tokens and hundreds of tool calls. Twice a year, Scott advertises upcoming meetups and makes a bigger deal about it than usual. Throughout the year his meetup czar (that’s me, Skyler!) gets emails from people moving to a new city wondering if there’s an ACX group there. So the twice a year Times & Places posts are a helpful chance to check for signs of life and get an update on the local meetup communities. But the most important part is coordination. If you only go to one ACX meetup a year, we suggest you go to the fall ACX Everywhere in your city. That way if there was secretly a dozen of you all making the assumption that you were the only reader in the area, you could all show up at the fall meetup and realize the conspiracy was larger than you thought. And in fact many local ACX groups got their start by just such a rallying flag. A few were even started by a traveling reader who volunteered to run a meetup in a city they didn’t live in, but locals showed up, took the banner, and kept the meetup going. This year we have meetups planned in over a hundred and eighty cities, from Aachen, Germany to Zagreb, Croatia. items.title: AI Safety Is Not A Corporate Plot
items.excerpt: AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have long mentioned the possibility that their products could be existentially dangerous, but this has recently crescendoed into even more dire warnings, including suggestions that we have to pace the frontier , ie coordinate to slow AI progress. In response, cynical commentators have suggested this is a conspiracy to boost the companies’ stocks. The exact motives imputed vary from person to person. Some say the companies are hyping the product by talking about how dangerous it is; if AI is smart enough to kill all humans, it must be smart enough for your business workflow. Others say they’re trying to distract from near-term harms; every inch of newspaper space devoted to human extinction is one less inch that can be spent on plagiarism and water use. But the most popular story involves regulatory capture: if the product is unsafe, maybe it can only be trusted to a few big politically-connected companies, and everyone else should be banned. Many debates about AI are complicated and hard to resolve, but this one isn’t: all of these stories are clearly false. Some evidence: The AI experts who aren’t affiliated with big companies are just as concerned as the ones who are. The AI company leaders giving these warnings were giving the exact same warnings before they had AI companies - and in many cases, before they worked in the industry, or before the industry existed. If these corporate plots were real, they would be incredibly dumb.…

I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked ] In 1940 the Empire State Building was the tallest man-made structure in the world, and if you stood at the top of it you could see the future. Specifically, you could see this: the first NBC television broadcast transmitter, intermittently blasting 49.75 MHz audio and 46.5 MHz video signals across a hundred-mile swath of megalopolis. A turnstile antenna, a ring of linked dipoles, and a crowning lightning rod formed the sharp point at the literal apex of human achievement. This is the lance that scraped the sky deeper than it had ever been scraped, the tip of the spear for a high radio modernism that would soon conquer the world. This is the needle that pierced the veil of the corporeal and pulled the thread of human culture into a realm of deracinated ghosts forever haunting the invisible airwaves. Maybe this sounds overwrought and spooky. But I’m not just editorializing on my own here: this is how some of the guys who invented television talked about it! I found this out by reading We Present Television , a collection of essays by various stakeholders in the earliest American TV broadcast systems—“televisionaries”, as they are occasionally referred to in the text. items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: CJC-1295 Explained: Does It Really Increase Growth Hormone?
items.excerpt: Does CJC-1295 really increase growth hormone? 🧬 CJC-1295 is often discussed alongside growth hormone, muscle growth, fat loss, recovery, and anti-aging—but CJC-1295 is not growth hormone. It's a synthetic analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) designed to stimulate the pituitary gland, which can increase the body's own release of growth hormone (GH) and raise IGF-1 levels. Early human research involving the long-acting DAC form of CJC-1295 found that a single dose produced sustained increases in average growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. But there's an important distinction: Increasing GH and IGF-1 does NOT automatically prove that CJC-1295 builds muscle, burns fat, improves longevity, or reverses aging. Changing a biomarker and demonstrating a meaningful clinical benefit are two very different things. In this Peptide A to Z Short, we break down what CJC-1295 actually does, how the pituitary → GH → IGF-1 pathway works, and why it's important to separate human research from claims made online. 🧬 Follow Peptide A to Z for evidence-based coverage of peptides, clinical trials, longevity science, GLP-1 research, and emerging compounds. items.title: Developing Gemini 4 Argon responsibly and safely
Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
items.excerpt: For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine. AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls. We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different. AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. items.title: Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org
items.excerpt: Working with outside collaborators can add more work for a repository owner. You need to confirm who still needs access, change permissions as projects evolve, and archive repositories once they’ve served their purpose. To keep up, repository owners need to track collaborators, deadlines, and follow-ups for each repository. As a project grows, that manual housekeeping becomes harder to keep up with and easier to defer. We faced this problem in a shared organization where GitHub employees (“Hubbers”) collaborate with customers and partners on product trials and professional services engagements. Our answer was Evergreen , a GitHub App built with native GitHub features. The workflows below exhibit a pattern you can adapt for your own organization. Meet Evergreen Evergreen is a GitHub App that automates organization hygiene through two workflows: Outside collaborator access reviews. Every quarter, each repo’s outside collaborators are reviewed. Keep who you need, and everyone else is removed. Stale repository detection and archival. Repos with no human activity past a threshold get flagged, warned, and (if still untouched) archived. Two design principles shaped everything: Fail secure. If nobody responds to an access review, we don’t leave access in place and hope for the best. We revoke it. The safe outcome is the default outcome. Never destroy anything. Evergreen will never delete a repository or its contents. Archived repos are recoverable, and every access change is written…

items.title: GitHub availability report: September 2026
items.excerpt: Our last update covered content through August. We did not publish another in September while other public content addressed the August 17 outage. This edition covers progress over the past two months. The short version of August and September : we reduced shared-database pressure, added overload controls, created headroom for GitHub Actions, expanded failure containment for pull requests, and moved more production workloads to Azure. Significant incidents, a capacity pause, and a missed migration target show that the work is not complete. By October 7, 120 of 160 production services were deployed in Central US, and 13 of 51 primary MySQL databases had moved. Azure also handled 65.4% of read traffic for GitHub’s core application, 48.3% of Git read traffic, and 80.2% of stream-processing traffic. These percentages measure different workloads and should not be added. We paused Central US deployments and traffic increases on September 11 because capacity was uneven across availability zones. Permanent ramps resumed September 18 after temporary relief, but durable capacity work continues, with a goal of unlocking all available capacity by the end of October. We missed our aggressive September 30 goal to deploy every production service there. During a planned database failover, an automated emergency process disconnected Central US database copies and disrupted customers in that region. items.title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers
items.excerpt: Maintainers look at star history to answer a practical question: did a launch, release, or event change a project’s trajectory? To reconstruct that curve from the GitHub API, tools had to request pages of stargazer records (each person who currently stars the repository and when they starred it), keep the timestamps, and throw the identities away. Over time, that design created problems at both ends. Identities were available for bulk collection, so bad actors started scraping public stargazer lists for spam and phishing campaigns. For highly starred repositories, the endpoint could also make the database process many thousands of entries to return a single page. The fix seemed clear: return counts instead of people. But returning less data didn’t actually make the query any cheaper. Now maintainers have a direct way to get the curve: we built an endpoint that returns up to 30 weeks of daily star counts in a single request, with no identities attached. Keeping that cheap to serve meant reducing how much data the database processed, not just how much it returned, and the endpoint does that by filtering stars by time before it counts anything . What maintainers need from star history We first addressed the immediate risks to developers and to our database by restricting stargazer and watcher lists to repository administrators and collaborators . Can Foreign Capital Count as Private Financing for Purposes of SSBCI Rules? [7/22/2026] Yes. Loans and investments may count toward SSBCI requirements if they are from a private source as described in Section VIII.b of the Guidelines, even if that source originates outside of the United States. In accordance with Presidential Memorandum dated February 21, 2025, it is the policy of the United States to preserve an open investment environment and Treasury encourages investments that will magnify federal SSBCI funding and support American small businesses. The transaction, including the use of the private financing, must otherwise comply with all SSBCI requirements and any other applicable state, local, or federal law, including Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) filing requirements that may be triggered (see, 31 CFR Parts 800 and 802). Participating jurisdictions should be mindful of these requirements and should communicate the same to their participating providers. In particular, while investment from a foreign sovereign wealth fund will qualify as private financing for purposes of SSBCI requirements (i.e., it does not originate from a domestic public source such as a state, federal, or Tribal government), such investments may be within CFIUS jurisdiction for purposes of CFIUS review. While Treasury will make reasonable efforts to process all pending disbursement requests prior to September 30, 2030, disbursement requests submitted after June 30, 2030, are not expected to be processed. items.title: Hybrid sales rise while battery electric sales remain lower after tax credit expiration
items.excerpt: In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26), 23% of new light-duty vehicles sold in the United States were hybrid electric, battery electric, or plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, down slightly from 24% in 3Q25. Between 3Q25 and 3Q26, hybrid electric vehicles continued to gain market share, reaching 16% of light-duty vehicle sales. Growth of hybrid electric vehicle sales has slowed this quarter as the average transaction price for a new vehicle passed $50,000-the first time this price has been reached so far this year, according to Kelley Blue Book.

items.title: U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade
items.excerpt: We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country-California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida-are in regions with more abundant solar resources. Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives.

items.title: Drug company gifts, meals, and payments to doctors lead to worse prescribing, review of 93 studies finds
items.excerpt: Key findings Pharmaceutical marketing aimed at doctors, from gifts to meals and payments, may increase inappropriate prescribing and the quantity and cost of prescriptions. Conflict‐of‐interest policies that restrict or manage interactions between pharmaceutical companies and doctors can limit prescribing of inappropriate drugs and overprescribing. Gifts, payments, free meals, and other marketing ploys by pharmaceutical companies heavily influence doctors to prescribe more drugs, choose less appropriate treatments, and drive up prescription costs, according to a systematic review of 93 studies. These prescribing choices can expose patients to drugs that offer fewer benefits, cause more side effects or are unnecessary, while increasing health system costs. The review , published today [October 9] in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, found that policies restricting interactions between drug companies and doctors were associated with better prescribing choices, lower costs, and possibly fewer prescriptions. “Overall, when doctors have more contact with drug company promotion, prescribing tends to become less appropriate, more frequent, and more expensive,” said co-author Dr. Lisa Bero, an affiliate professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Center of Bioethics and Humanities. “This is problematic for a number of reasons, and it matters because it directly affects patient care.” Dr. Quinn Grundy, director of the World Health Organization Collaborating Centre for…

items.title: Hormone-disrupting chemical mixtures linked to excess childhood weight
items.excerpt: Key findings Multiple hormone-disrupting chemicals were linked to obesity from childhood through adolescence. Prenatal exposure to metals, organochlorine pesticides, and PFAS was linked to higher obesity. Childhood exposure to phenols and certain phthalates was linked to more body fat in adolescence. Children exposed during pregnancy and early life to combinations of chemicals that disrupt hormones and metabolism may face a greater risk of excess weight that persists into adolescence, a new study suggests. Published this month [September 2026] in Environment International , the study followed 1,301 mother-child pairs from six European birth cohorts. Researchers measured prenatal and childhood exposure to 45 endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) across nine chemical classes. These included per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances ( PFAS), phthalates , pesticides , polychlorinated biphenyls ( PCBs), flame retardants, metals, parabens, and phenols, including bisphenol A (BPA) and triclosan. Researchers found that greater exposure to certain combinations of EDCs was associated with higher BMI. They also found links to more body fat and higher odds of overweight. About 28% of the children had overweight or obesity at age 8, rising to about 30% by age 15. The findings add to growing evidence linking chemical exposures during critical stages of development to obesity risk.
